label: Zamorano-Leonese

links.name: Albertos et al. 2022, Frontiers in Nutrition

names.text: Alternative names Carbajalina, Leonesa, Zamorana, Garañón Leonés and Asno zamorano-leonés are from the Wikipedia article, which cites the Spanish ministry (MAPA) breed sheet. Zamorano-Leonesa and Zamorano-Leonés are the spellings used in the Frontiers paper. Asno Zamorano-Leonés and Zamorano Leonés come from the item's known record and the same Frontiers paper.

about.text: The Zamorano-Leonese is an endangered Spanish donkey breed from the provinces of Zamora and León in Castilla y León, north-western Spain. Formerly kept as a working and pack animal, it is now small in number and mostly kept in its home region. Its milk was characterised in 2022 as a possible protein food, proposed as a way to conserve the breed.

links.name: Albertos et al. 2022, Frontiers in Nutrition

sources.text: Origin in Zamora and León, the former working use, and the 'most in Castilla y León' population share come from the Wikipedia article (citing MAPA 2014 and Fernández Rodríguez et al. 2009). The endangered status and the milk-characterisation proposal come from the Frontiers paper, which describes the breed as a protected endangered species and says the best way to preserve it is to explore milk production. 'Small in number' rests on the 1,292 registered head (2013).

origin.place: The provinces of Zamora and León, Castilla y León, north-western Spain

sources.text: The article says the breed comes 'from the provinces of Zamora and León, in the autonomous community of Castilla y León', and that donkeys in Zamora 'date back to at least the fifteenth century' (citing MAPA, accessed July 2014). No formation date is given, so 'formed' is left out.

'At the end of 2013 the registered population was 1292 head, of which about 90% were in Castilla y León', citing MAPA, 'Raza equino asnal ZAMORANO-LEONÉS: Datos censales' (accessed July 2014). Taken from the Wikipedia article, not from the MAPA page directly.

'The donkeys were formerly kept as working animals, both for animal traction and as pack animals' (citing Fernández Rodríguez et al. 2009, Guía de campo de las razas autóctonas españolas, p. 440). Jacks were mainly used to produce large mules for agricultural work. Milk is not listed as a use in this source; it is a proposed new use in the Frontiers paper.

links.name: Albertos et al. 2022, Frontiers in Nutrition

sources.text: FAO 2007 'endangered', citing Rischkowsky and Pilling (eds.), List of breeds documented in the Global Databank for Animal Genetic Resources (FAO, 2007), as given in the Wikipedia article. The 2022 Frontiers paper calls it a protected endangered species. The current DAD-IS entry was not reached, so this may be out of date; the SAVE 2008 rating of 'stable' is noted in the article but not used here.

facts.v: Its milk was characterised in 2022 as an alternative protein food, with the authors proposing milk production as a way to preserve the breed.

links.name: Albertos et al. 2022, Frontiers in Nutrition

sources.text: Title: 'Characterisation of Zamorano-Leonese Donkey Milk as an Alternative Sustainably Produced Protein Food' (Albertos I, López M, Jiménez JM, Cao MJ, Corell A, Castro-Alija MJ; Frontiers in Nutrition 9, published 8 April 2022). Taken from the paper's text: 'The best way to preserve it is to explore viable alternatives such as milk production.'

facts.v: Jacks were mainly used to produce large mules for agricultural work.

sources.text: From the Wikipedia article, citing Fernández Rodríguez et al. 2009, p. 440.

facts.v: Donkeys in the province of Zamora date back to at least the fifteenth century.

sources.text: From the Wikipedia article, citing MAPA, 'Raza equino asnal ZAMORANO-LEONÉS', accessed July 2014.

gaps: Yield per lactation, lactation length and a yield per year were not found; the paper gives only a daily milking note (two litres a day after about six weeks) and jennies sampled at 60 to 120 days of lactation. Formation date not found. The current DAD-IS breed entry was not reached (the FAO browse page returned 404), so the risk status is the 2007 FAO listing as quoted secondhand; the population figure is the 2013 registered count. Later counts conflict: the Frontiers paper (2022) says 1,448 donkeys in Spain, unclear whether breed or national total, and an Agronews article dated 29 December 2016 says about 1,500 animals without a clear year. Composition: the paper's Results text and Table 5 disagree on which of fat (0.56) and protein (1.68) is which; Table 5 was used. Total solids are not reported; about 9.05 % can be worked out from the reported moisture of 90.95 %, but it is left out as it is not a sourced figure. Milk production in the 2022 paper is described as a proposal, not a current use.
